title: When several edge finders disagree on the same frame, the disagreement is the measurement uncertainty
summary: Each segmentation method draws a different outline around the same flame because 'where the edge is' depends on a rule. Overlaying all of them on one real frame shows which rules agree, which depend on the glow, and which fail.

media.alt: A real frame of a bright flame on a dark background with five coloured outlines overlaid. A tight cyan outline hugs the visible flame. A yellow outline is a much wider halo around it. A magenta outline is a large blocky shape extending above the frame into the white margin. An orange outline is a stepped, blocky shape close to the flame. A white outline is a ragged fragment to the right of the flame. A dashed red line marks the burner exit.

read_the_figure.question: Do different ways of finding the flame edge give the same outline on the same real frame, and where do they not?
read_the_figure.axes: No data axes: a photograph with overlays. Each coloured outline is the boundary of the flame region found by one method; the legend (top right) lists the method names. The dashed red horizontal line near the bottom is the burner exit reference. The title gives the run, the regime, the time and the frame number.
look_at: The cyan outline, labelled incumbent: it follows the bright core and the visible tip closely in both frames.
The yellow (luma) outline: a smooth oval well outside the bright core, tracing the faint glow. Its width is far larger than the visible flame, so any width measured with it is inflated.
The magenta (chroma) outline: a large rectangular shape with straight vertical sides that extends above the picture area in the onset frame. It is not tracing the flame at all in these two frames.
The orange (hysteresis) outline: close to the flame but with stepped, blocky edges; in the onset frame it has a diagonal cut across the flame.
The white (temporal) outline: a ragged fragment away from the flame in the onset frame, and absent as a clean closed shape.
The green outline (diffmat), only in the developed-puffing frame: it follows part of the right edge of the upper flame and stops, so it is incomplete.
read_the_figure.proves: That edge position is a property of the method as much as of the flame, and that agreement of several methods within a small band supports a measurement while large disagreement means the quantity is not well defined. Two real frames cannot show which method is most accurate over a campaign.
if_wrong: An outline much wider than the visible flame: the threshold sits in the glow.
An outline with straight vertical or horizontal edges: a bounding box or a region grown from a coarse mask, not an edge.
An outline that runs outside the image or is open: the method did not close a contour.
A fragment disconnected from the flame: noise or background structure passed the criterion.
must_check: That all outlines are drawn on the same frame and in the same coordinate system.
Any reference mask or ground truth: none is shown, so 'better' is a judgment from the picture.
The number of frames compared: here, one per figure.
The saturation of the camera: the white core is clipped, so the true intensity profile near the core is lost.
Whether a method was tuned on the frame it is shown on.
as_drawn: Method names in the legend: incumbent, luma, chroma, hysteresis, temporal, and diffmat in the second frame. No ranking or score is shown, and none is taught here.
MVI_8036 onset frame at t = 175.0 s is frame 4196, which corresponds to 24 frames per second; the developed-puffing frame is at t = 300.0 s, frame 7193.
The yellow outline in the onset frame is about 400 px wide, against about 160 px for the cyan one, read by eye at the image size.

terms.meaning: Assigning each pixel to flame or background. The boundary of the flame region is the outline drawn.
An intensity level above which a pixel counts as flame. Moving it moves the edge.
Brightness and colour components of a video pixel. A luma method thresholds brightness; a chroma method thresholds colour.
Two thresholds: pixels above the high one are flame, and pixels between the two count only if connected to the high ones. It suppresses isolated noise.
A method that uses several consecutive frames (for example differences between frames) rather than one image.
Light scattered around the flame by the optics and the air. It makes the apparent edge soft.
Pixels at the maximum value of the sensor; information above that level is lost.
How a point of light is blurred by the optics; a sharp edge becomes a smooth ramp of width about sigma.

remember: The edge of a blurred object is wherever you set the threshold.
A threshold at fraction f of the plateau shifts the edge by sigma times the inverse normal CDF of f for a Gaussian-blurred step.
Different methods are different definitions, not different accuracies of one definition.
Overlays on a real frame are a sanity check, not a score.
Two frames are an illustration, not a validation.
Always ask which outline a published width or height came from.

understand.title: Why the outlines differ
understand.text: Each method answers a different question: where is it bright, where is it a different colour, where is it connected to the bright core, where did something move. For a soft-edged luminous object these questions have different answers, so the outlines differ by many millimetres.

understand.title: Why overlay on one frame
understand.text: It removes every excuse: same pixels, same moment. You can judge by eye which outline follows the visible edge and which does not, before any statistic is computed.

understand.title: Why the developed-puffing frame is harder
understand.text: In the onset frame the flame is a symmetric tongue; in the puffing frame the upper part detaches and curves, and thin bright filaments lie beside the main body. Methods that rely on connectedness or on a fixed threshold are most likely to disagree there.

steps.title: A blurred step edge
steps.note: Model of a sharp edge at x0 seen through optics with a Gaussian blur of width sigma; Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

steps.title: Edge position for a threshold
steps.note: A threshold at fraction f of the plateau places the edge at x0 plus a shift. At f = 0.5 the shift is zero.

steps.title: How much a low threshold moves the edge
steps.note: For f = 0.2 the edge moves outward by about 0.84 sigma (value of the inverse normal CDF computed numerically). On both sides the apparent width grows by about 1.7 sigma.

steps.title: Otsu's choice of a single threshold
steps.note: Standard automatic threshold: choose the level that maximises the between-class variance of the two pixel groups below and above it, where omega are the group fractions and mu their mean intensities.

steps.title: Hysteresis thresholding
steps.tex: p\in F\iff I(p)>\theta_{H}\ \text{ or }\ \bigl(I(p)>\theta_{L}\ \text{and } p \text{ is connected to } F\bigr)
steps.note: Pixels above the high level are flame; pixels above the low level are flame only if connected to them. It removes isolated bright specks but can follow glow if the low level is too low.

worked.title: How far does a glow-level threshold move the edge
worked.problem: The optics blur a sharp flame edge with a Gaussian of sigma = 2 mm in the image. A method thresholds at 20 percent of the plateau. By how much is the edge moved outward, and how much wider does a flame of true width 10 mm look?

solution.text: The inverse normal CDF at 0.2 is about -0.842, so the shift is 0.842 sigma.

worked.answer: About 1.7 mm per side, so the flame appears about 13.4 mm wide instead of 10 mm. The sigma and widths are made-up teaching numbers.

analyze.q: Why does the yellow outline hug the glow while the cyan outline hugs the bright core? What parameter of the method would move the yellow one inward?
The magenta outline leaves the picture area in the onset frame. List two ways a method can produce such a result and say what you would inspect.
analyze.hint: Colour mask of a reflective background; region growing without a bound.

analyze.q: A width measured with the yellow method is inflated. Does it also change the fluctuation (RMS) of the width in time, or only the mean?
analyze.hint: A constant offset has no variance; a threshold-dependent offset that varies does.

evaluate.q: Do two frames validate a method? What evidence would?
evaluate.hint: Many frames, hand-drawn reference outlines, an overlap score, stated uncertainty.

evaluate.q: The caption says earlier method rankings were superseded. How should a reader treat any ranking that predates a correction?
evaluate.hint: As not current: ask for the date and the scoreboard version.

create: Design a test with hand-drawn reference outlines on 50 frames spread over regimes, and a score that treats the glow fairly.
Draw an overlay figure that stays readable for eight methods, using line style as well as colour.

checks.q: Why do the outlines differ if they are all from the same frame?
checks.answer: Because each method defines the edge by a different rule, and for a soft, glowing edge those rules give different positions.

checks.q: A Gaussian-blurred edge with sigma 3 px is thresholded at 20 percent. How far does the edge move?
The magenta outline has straight sides. What does that suggest?
checks.hint: Edges of a physical flame are not straight.
checks.answer: It is a bounding region or a coarse mask, not an edge found from the flame's intensity; it should not be used as a flame boundary in these frames.

checks.q: Can you say from this figure which method is best?
checks.answer: No. It is one frame per figure, with no reference outline. It supports a visual sanity check only.

checks.q: How would you quantify disagreement between two outlines?
checks.answer: Use the intersection over union of the two regions, and the mean and maximum distance between the contours, computed over many frames.
